idiom_name: asyncio event loop with loop.run_in_executor / asyncio.to_thread and asyncio.Queue
implementation_notes: asyncio supplies both layers: the selector-based event loop is the asynchronous layer, and loop.run_in_executor() - whose default executor is a lazily initialised ThreadPoolExecutor - is the documented way to run blocking code off the loop, since asyncio has no asynchronous file I/O and points at run_in_executor for exactly that. asyncio.Queue is the queueing layer for the explicit worker-pool shape: a fixed number of tasks drain it with await queue.get() while producers enqueue from coroutines or, from executor threads, via loop.call_soon_threadsafe. The pure threading structure (queue.Queue plus worker threads) remains right when no coroutine ever touches the pipeline.
code_sketch:
async def on_conn(reader, writer):                       # asynchronous layer
    await q.put((reader, writer))
q = asyncio.Queue(maxsize=1024)                           # queueing layer
async def consume():
    while True:
        reader, writer = await q.get()
        await asyncio.to_thread(handle_blocking, reader, writer)   # synchronous layer
async def main():
    server = await asyncio.start_server(on_conn, host, 8080)
    [asyncio.create_task(consume()) for _ in range(4)]
    async with server:
        await server.serve_forever()
pitfalls: A blocking call inside a coroutine (time.sleep, requests, a synchronous database driver) freezes the whole loop unless it is wrapped in asyncio.to_thread or run_in_executor.
The default executor is process-wide and its worker count is a shared resource; a burst of to_thread calls can starve other components.
Executor threads must hand results back with loop.call_soon_threadsafe rather than touching asyncio objects directly, which is not thread-safe.
Cancelling the awaiting coroutine does not stop the thread already running the blocking function.
